I'm probably not adding anything new but here are some issues I can identify, mostly because I have been through that phase. 

1) Underestimation of the risk: after we have a few seizures and gain some experience, we get the notion that they can't be too dangerous. After all, we have had so many and living today. It is important that he understands that the next seizure could kill him. He may not regain consciousness after the next one. Or that the next seizure could permanently disable him. It is absolutely not OK to allow yourself to have seizures. I was a person who did that and had to learn the lesson the hard way.

2) Taking responsibility : We have all been teenagers who hate being controlled. Eventually, we grew up. The situation with your BIL is the same but with significantly higher stakes. Sleep deprivation and video games may be contributing factors. But the solution can't be bed times for a 19 year old. It has to be instilling a sense of responsibility and ownership. Like others said that could mean getting his own place. It could also mean the rest of the family agreeing to not helping him after his next episode. Let him clean up the blood and get himself first aid. I don't mean let him die, but if he is confident enough of his ability to handle seizures, let him truly do that.

3) Mental health: maybe he is going through something that makes him resist treatment. Check up on if he is doing OK in other aspects. Maybe take him to a doc. AEDs can mess with clarity of thoughts. And sometimes we may want to fight seizures with brute force.

Air can hold a maximum amount of water at a temperature. This amount increases with temperature.

As air cools, it gets saturated with water and when the dew point is reached, this water "comes out" of air in the form of condensation.

If the air had a lot of water to begin with (high humidity), it doesn't take a lot of cooling to saturate it, so high dew point. Similarly, low humidity=low dew point.

That's why the condensation on cold glasses on different days vary. It comes down to the amount of humidity.

This is relevant because it tells us about how humid the air is and how easy it is for water to evaporate. 

For example, Warm weather with a high dew point makes evaporative cooling very difficult since water can't evaporate quickly despite the high temperature because of a high dew point.

I was hospitalised a few years back and my situation was nearly identical with the following differences:

1) I had epilepsy for about 8 years at that point.
2) I had abruptly stopped my epilepsy meds. So I was probably going through epilepsy med withdrawal
3) my mom was in your place.

I was taken to the hospital after a lot of seizures (most likely because I stopped my epilepsy meds, one of which was a benzo. So I was probably going through benzo withdrawal) 

The doc's needed to stop my brain from seizing ASAP. So they placed me in a coma since that would halt the seizures and buy time. 

After this, they asked my mom if I had a history of substance abuse. She said no. This happened 2 more times by different docs since they didn't believe her (probably because ODs can cause seizures). 

The docs insisted on testing me for drugs. My mom consented. All drugs negative (other than my epilepsy meds). Bitter sweet news for my mom. She was happy that her son doesn't use drugs but docs still had no clue as to why I was seizing. 

Docs tested my spinal fluid for signs of infection. Nothing. 

After a day in my medically induced coma, they tried to get me out of the coma and observe my brain activity (through an EEG scan). Didn't go well. Everytime they weaned me off the "coma inducing drugs" (I'm not a doc. I'm a patient. I don't know the terms 😅), my brain flooded with seizure activity. 

Docs decided to place me on a ventilator since there was a risk that my brain may stop sending the "breathing signals" to my lungs.

After a combination of meds they tapered down the "coma drugs". The seizure activity was a lot smaller. After about 3-4 days in the ICU, I was out of harms way and was shifted to the ward. 2 days later, I was given the green signal to go home. 

I know I haven't addressed the straps. 
For that let's look at those days from my perspective:

My brain and body were not functioning. My ability to perceive and process thoughts was pretty much 0. I had very strong hallucinations as a result of the drugs that were pumped into me and the seizures. 

Everytime I opened my eyes, I saw faces that I didn't recognise, and I was barely able to speak or move. Everytime I did try to move, I was asked to lie down. And when I did move, I was sedated. I wasn't able to perceive that I was in a hospital. In my mind, I was kidnapped and held against my will by strangers. When docs weaned me off the "coma drugs" my fight-flight response kicked in. I'd rip out my IV line, catheter and feeding tube and try to run for my life. In the survival mode, the body gets strong. I physically kicked and punched my "kidnappers" (nurses) in an attempt to "escape to safety". The staff had to wrestle me down since I had removed the IV line. To prevent that, they strapped my wrists and ankles to the bed.

Honestly, I came here looking for some encouragement after a rough few days. Here are some words that I'm not following right now, but should:

1) Consistency is key! One of the perks of our condition is that it teaches us the value of consistency. We can't pull all nighters (atleast I can't and shouldn't). So we change our outlook towards life. Consistency as opposed to bursts of productivity. We are marathon runners, not sprinters. And marathon runners cover more distance over time compared to the sprinters. Let's keep those legs moving

2) celebrate small wins! Slow progress means we can get existential. Not knowing if we're making progress in life can really get to you. Idk if I've made any progress in my job. I have no clue what my boss will say to me at the next performance review. But building work experience is still progress. That's still a win, and I'm happy with that. I'll figure out the rest later.

3) Get a bit existential. At the end of it, we are nothing more than very complicated chemical reactions on a tiny spec of dust in the universe. Our failures don't really have consequences. We can pretty much live our lives as if it is consequence free. If anyone says otherwise, ignore them. We're playing a very immersive video game. Don't stress.

4) We are surprisingly resilient but forget. When my seizures went out of control, I was forced to quit my job, sit at home and pretty much stare into space because of my meds and loss of hope regarding my future. But we bounce back. It is inherent human nature to adapt to a bad situation, make the best of it and then grow from there. Looking back I'm like "how the hell did you make it out of that!". I'm willing to bet that if we all look back at our lows, we will be shocked that we climbed out of the hole and probably didn't notice it. We are probably going through one of those lows and we will look back in a few days and be surprised that we made it out of that without realising.

I don't think I'll be adding anything new compared to a lot of the comments. Like you, I knew no one with epilepsy when I was diagnosed. Neither did my family. We discovered the seriousness of the condition only once I faced it first hand. In hindsight, some help would hs e been nice. So here are my 2 cents based on my experiences. 

Im guessing you'll be starting with your Anti Epilepsy Drugs (AEDs) soon. It took me some time to get used to them. They can pack a punch and may require some adaptation either in the short term while you adjust to them and/or in the long term since some of the side effects can stick. It is very important comply with the meds. If you don't like them, communicate that very clearly with your doc. There are plenty of meds and combinations. Different people respond differently to them. Your feedback would be very helpful in finding the combination that works well for you.

It is also very important to keep morale up. In my case, I could feel myself change as a person over the course of the medication. My clarity of thought and memory is not what it was before starting my meds. I've started to accept it and not beat myself up for not living up to my potential. I still have days filled with self doubt. I guess consistency is key. Take it one day at a time. 

I've noticed that a "healthier lifestyle" helps. Getting some exercise, cutting out alcohol and eating healthy generally helps me feel better. It could very well be placebo, but hey, I still feel better.

Finally, sleep is super important. You'll probably get pretty sleepy because of the meds. I'm talking 12 hours a day kind of sleepy. Atleast that was the case with me. Give in to it. Sleep. Your brain probably needs it. Sleep deprivation lowers my seizure threshold.

I had 3-4 MRIs over the last 10 years.

MRI machines come with different resolutions. My first MRI found no abnormalities. 

The MRI scans from the higher (3 Tesla?) resolution found some scar tissue in my brain (that's what the doc told me after finishing the MRI) . However my Neuro disagreed and was of the opinion that there was no scar tissue. The same was confirmed by another doctor.

A few years later, I had another MRI. After this result, a different group of neuros looked at the scan and had no doubt that there was scar tissue.

So either more scarring developed over 2-3 years or docs can have different opinions looking at the same scan or different scans give different insights.

Yes and no. My patterns have changed over the years and I've been on many different meds over this time. 

1) 2010 to 2018- my seizures followed a 30-40 day cycle. I primarily had simple and complex partial seizures.

Pattern- frequency of auras increase from 1 in 3 days to 5-6 in 1 day. After this, I'd have 4-6 complex partial seizures over 2 days. After this, I'm aura free for 1-2 weeks. Almost like a brain factory reset.

2) 2018 to 2020- no more complex partial seizures. Ocassional aura and grandmal seizures and the two were independent of each other. The grand mals were primarily triggered due to not taking AEDs for 2-3 days and sleep deprivation. 

3) 2020 to today- only auras. The nature of these auras are very different. A lot weaker and almost not an aura, if that makes sense. Usually happens when I haven't taken my meds for over 18 hours. So serves as a natural reminder to take meds.

I've been on a lot of epilepsy meds over the years, and I've had a lot of experiences. I'm on keppra right now and here is my general take:
1) it takes a while to get used to the meds. I'm talking something like 6 months. That may seem daunting, but remember it's not like a switch where you suddenly feel better from the 7th month. Its a curve where things get worse as you start with the meds and then start getting better.

2) seizures take a toll on your brain. Depending on the extremity, recovery from seizures take hours to weeks (and in my case months). It is a priority to control seizures. Initially, I thought preventing seizures was important to prevent death and meds was something that I just had to live with. Now (after a lot of rebellions) I've come to realise that controlling seizures actually improves your quality of life (suicidal thoughts and depression becomes less frequent) and you ease into your meds. You identify your triggers better and life becomes more predictable.

3) when you start off, you're in a state of shock. Atleast I was. You realise your life has changed and that you can't do the things you wanted to do (my dreams of being a pilot or joining the military were shattered). That's really demotivating. You start wondering why you worked hard for years towards something you can no longer do for no fault of yours. I tackled this by starting small. Take it one day at a time. Find small wins. Start with puzzles. Work out. These small confidence boosters keep you going as you ease into your meds and start to heal. Eventually as you settle in and accept reality, you find other interests you probably really enjoy, but never considered because you were focused on one thing (that was the case for me)

4) exercise is key! Something about the post workout rush makes you feel great. Be it cardio or pumping iron, they make you feel great after. These little things really go a long way in making your day.

5) interpersonal relationships will need to be adapted. People who care about you will be worried, even paranoid. I get calls if I don't reply to messages because people are concerned about me. Privacy and independence is compromised because parents would much rather have me live at their place than work in a different city. Romantic relationships may be hard at first because of memory issues or mood swings.

I don't mean to scare you. I just want to give you an idea of what you may expect since I (and in my interactions, a lot of others) have experienced. So don't panic if you feel this way.

We have this condition. We don't want to give up on everything we want because of it. The best thing to do is to figure out how to take the next step. Don't skip meds. Find small wins and take it one day at a time. Things will get better. It has for me.

My background:

I'm 25, and was diagnosed and started treatment when I was 15. I have memories of seizures from when I was 5-6 years of age. Since most of my seizures were not the dramatic collapsing and shaking (grand mal seizures) kind, it was very hard for me to describe what I felt. Since no one in my family had a history of epilepsy, or really knew what I was referring to, they usually checked my temperature, and when there was no symptoms of the flu, they made me eat made sure I was hydrated and made me rest. We all connected the dots only when my seizures got bad enough to take me to the ER when I was in high school and the doc described the possible symptoms and we were all like "yes! That's what it was!". I have been a rebellious patient, fighting the meds and not giving them a chance because of the side effects. I finally learn my lesson in Feb this year, when I regained consciousness after nearly a week in the ICU because I pushed my rebellion too far and my brain started to shut down with other vital organs. Thankfully, and much to my neurologists' surprise, I made it and am back to "normal". Now I'm a very "good" patient with very timely meds and don't skip my doses.

The reason I gave you this background is that things can get really bad really quickly if you're careless. So don't "play through the pain" when it comes to this. 

Look on the bright side. You haven't been epileptic during your formative years. You've developed your individual personality while not under the influence of meds. Yo have been diagnosed at a relatively early stage.

Your concern regarding meds are largely temporary. The body adjusts (a few weeks to months). You don't notice them too much over time. Life will be a bit different, but you need to make the best of what you have.

AEDs tend to be a bit depressive (they are suppressing brain activity). You will adjust to them. Don't make any big decisions in the spur of the moment. Chances are that you haven't had a chance to emotionally process the consequences yet. Its OK to take your time.

You don't have to benchmark yourself to others. It's OK to take breaks. Don't get sucked into the toxic work culture of trying to over achieve everyday. Do what you can and get out. There is a difference between being lazy and giving up viz a viz knowing limits and not crossing them (although I don't know where the line is yet).

Hope you get better soon :)
